correctness.rationale: For all odd n≥3, digit decomposition r=(n-1)u+d yields S((n-1)x)=B S(x) exactly. On Fourier vector v_z, Bv_z=A(z)v_{z^-1}; B² eigenvalues are 0 for z=1 and -((z-1)/(z+1))² for z≠1. The finite odd-binomial expansion annihilates all nonconstant modes because z^n=1, and has value n at 0; thus P_n(B²)=J_n. This proves all n,i,x with no finite extrapolation. Included checker replays exact integer projector matrices for 12 odd n and direct digit sums; checker tests do not replace the proof. Boundaries n≥3 odd, i=0..n-1, x integer≥0 explicitly handled.

originality.rationale: The authors explicitly posed the all-residue, all-cutoff formula as Conjecture (74) and the residue-zero case as conjectural (15) in arXiv:1209.5705v3. They proved only n=3,5 and supplied an n-dependent checking method. Their earlier arXiv:1207.0404 established an odd-binomial polynomial for tangent squares but not the rank-one matrix projector on all residue partial sums. A new universal argument proves P_n(B^2)=J_n and therefore resolves both conjectures. Targeted literature and research-record searches found no already-proved identical statement; residual risk of unindexed equivalent proof remains.
residual_risks: A later independent proof or a general circulant-matrix theorem not indexed by searched literature could entail the same result; absence from search does not certify uniqueness.

The older paper provides necessary spectral polynomial and the conjecture paper supplies the digit transition; the result is a newly assembled universal argument rather than wholly new spectral theory.

value.rationale: The new matrix projector furnishes one uniform all-modulus proof of an explicitly conjectured infinite identity (arXiv:1209.5705v3 Eq. (74)), including full interval-residue vectors. It simultaneously discharges the original Eq. (15) and shows a dimension-independent collapse of (n+1)/2 signed digit-statistic transforms to total parity; the structurally meaningful proof connects a known tangent polynomial with arbitrary-prefix digit transforms, where prior work supplied only low-modulus proofs and computational tests.
